ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Billie Holiday Synthetic CCD — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

text.paragraph: Establishing primary care five weeks after release from custody: medication for opioid use disorder, overdose prevention, alcohol care, liver and infection screening, and depression and safety screening. Concerns: She wants to stay off heroin and keep singing, and is afraid of losing her tolerance and overdosing; She wants to drink less, especially around shows; She wants her records kept private and to be treated without judgment. [S]

list.item: Professional singer; returned to concert work and touring after her release; can no longer work in clubs in her home city because of a licensing rule tied to her conviction [S]

Returned home five weeks ago after about ten months in federal custody on a narcotics possession charge; no medication for opioid use disorder was offered there, and she has used no opioids since release [S]
Alcohol: four or five drinks on most performance nights since release (AUDIT-C 8); drinks to calm her nerves before and after shows [S]
Tobacco: about five cigarettes a day; not ready to stop now and knows help is available [S]
Supports: musicians she has worked with for years, a close friend who has agreed to carry naloxone, and a peer recovery coach; her music is her strongest source of purpose [S]

Has repeatedly been singled out by law enforcement and feels watched; wary of clinics and of anything written about her. Confidentiality under the federal substance use disorder privacy rule explained, and she decides what is shared [S]

tr.td: Establishing primary care five weeks after release from custody: medication for opioid use disorder, overdose prevention, alcohol care, liver and infection screening, and depression and safety screening
One-week buprenorphine check and addiction medicine consultation
Five-week recovery review and second hepatitis B vaccine
Three-month review after a return to opioid use: adjusting the recovery plan
Six-month recovery, alcohol, liver, and mood review
Same-day sick visit for a dental abscess

code.displayName: Periodic reevaluation and management of healthy individual

tr.td: Buprenorphine with naloxone started in primary care at a low first dose, then 16 mg daily, continued through any return to use; naloxone, overdose education, never using alone, and fentanyl test strips
Addiction medicine consultation to confirm the medication plan, choose a medicine for alcohol use disorder that can be used with buprenorphine, and set the monitoring plan
Alcohol care: acamprosate, thiamine, brief counseling and goals she chooses, and PEth at each check to follow drinking without relying on memory

Liver and infection screening: liver tests and FIB-4 at intake and six months, hepatitis C antibody, hepatitis B triple panel, and HIV test, with hepatitis A and B vaccines for a person who is not immune
Depression screening with the PHQ-9 at each recovery visit, a structured safety assessment with a written safety plan and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit
Integrated, trauma-informed recovery plan: weekly counseling, a peer recovery coach, confidentiality she controls, and a written plan for touring, without requiring recovery to be perfect or linear
Stay on buprenorphine without interruption through six months, including through any return to use
Taking buprenorphine 16 mg daily at six months; a three-day gap during a tour was followed by a brief return to use and an immediate restart, with no overdose
Naloxone at home and in her bag, and a friend trained to use it, by the one-week visit
Two naloxone two-packs dispensed; her friend trained
Reduce drinking to PEth below 20 ng/mL, or to the level she chooses, by six months
PEth 22 ng/mL from 312; occasional light drinking, which she chose
Hepatitis A and B vaccine series completed by six months
Hepatitis B doses at intake and five weeks; hepatitis A doses at intake and six months
PHQ-9 score below 5 by six months

list.item: Independent in all activities; performing several nights a week; sleep broken since release [S]
Alert, guarded at first and then candid; speech normal; no signs of intoxication or withdrawal [S]
Mood low and tired, with grief for her mother that still returns; PHQ-9 score 9 with item 9 scored 0; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 1948-04-20: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care. Overdose risk is high in the weeks after release because tolerance has fallen: naloxone for her and her friend, never using alone, testing any drug supply with fentanyl test strips, and buprenorphine started today. The 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline was given and saved in her phone, and a written safety plan was made with her. Safety reviewed at every visit [S]
